title: Every estimate ends in a design decision, or it gets dropped
caption: Five minutes, four to six numbers. Round hard at each step and say the unit.

steps.text: Say the assumptions out loud: DAU, actions per user, object size, retention, replicas.
Multiply to a daily volume, separately for reads and writes: 10 M users × 50 views = 500 M reads/day.
Divide by ~1e5 seconds per day: 500 M / 86 400 ≈ 5 800 reads/s on average.
Traffic isn't flat. Multiply by a peak factor: 5 800 × 3 ≈ 17 000 reads/s.
Storage = writes/day × size × days × replicas. Egress = QPS × bytes per response × 8 for bits.
Tie each number to a box: "17k reads/s → cache and replicas". A number that changes nothing wasted your time.

scenarios.name: Spiky traffic
scenarios.summary: Ticket sales, live events and pushes don't peak at 3× but at 10–100×: ask about the peak shape before picking a factor.

steps.text: Assume a ticket site: 1 M users who all arrive when sales open at 10:00.
Daily average ≈ 100 req/s, which looks tiny.
But the real peak is ~100× for 10 minutes: 10 000+ req/s. A ×3 factor would underbuild by 30×.
Design decision: a queue or waiting room in front, so the spike is admitted at a rate the backend can take.

scenarios.name: Risk: unit slip
scenarios.summary: Bits vs bytes or KB vs MB silently puts you 8× or 1 000× off. Write the unit on every number and sanity-check the result.

steps.text: Forget the ×8 and write "2.9 Gbps": one 10 Gbps NIC looks fine, but the real number is 23 Gbps.
The wrong number leads to the wrong decision: no CDN.
Say the unit every time ("gigabytes per second, times 8 is gigabits") and the CDN is obvious.
